claims.text: A compact, adherent iron oxide film formed during initial exposure controls the onset of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel.
A dense and uniform oxide layer suppresses further corrosion at both room and elevated temperatures.
A porous or inhomogeneous oxide film creates sites for localized galvanic reactions that accelerate degradation.
As-received Q235 steel has a thin, naturally formed oxide layer.
The naturally formed oxide layer on as-received Q235 steel is not optimized for passivity.
Controlled pre-oxidation in oxygen at a moderate temperature will promote a more uniform and dense oxide film.
The relevant surface oxide consists primarily of Fe2O3, with possible mixed iron oxides.
Oxide microstructure, thickness, porosity, and adhesion determine its effectiveness as a corrosion barrier.
A dense oxide barrier limits oxygen and electrolyte diffusion.
Restricted ionic transport and electron exchange suppress anodic iron dissolution.
An unstable, porous oxide permits pitting and crevice corrosion by enabling microgalvanic cells between intact metal and defective oxide sites.
Pre-oxidized Q235 steel will corrode more slowly than untreated Q235 steel under identical harsh environmental conditions.
Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit less mass loss than untreated samples.
Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit lower pit density than untreated samples.
Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit more stable passivation behavior in polarization testing than untreated samples.
The thin and possibly non-uniform natural oxide on untreated Q235 steel produces greater susceptibility to corrosion-related degradation.
Mechanical wear and long-term field exposure may disrupt or exceed the protection provided by the oxide film.
Humidity, chloride concentration, and oxygen availability can affect the protection produced by pre-oxidation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis begins by describing the material as 'pre-exposed Q235 steel,' whereas the material-initial-state field defines it as being in the 'pre-exposure' condition. These denote different exposure states unless 'pre-exposed' was intended to mean 'before exposure.'
